analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary cutoff for overtime pay to roughly $47,500 and updates it every three years.
analysis.headline: The overtime bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate labor committee from June 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal overtime law only protects salaried workers who make less than a set salary cutoff, and that cutoff had been stuck at $23,660 since the mid-2000s — below the poverty line for a family of four. This bill would write a higher cutoff into law: the 40th percentile of salaries in the lowest-wage region of the country (about $47,476 under the 2016 rule it incorporates), with automatic updates every three years so it stops falling behind wages. It would also require the government to publish quarterly data on salaried workers' earnings.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers who earn between the old $23,660 cutoff and the new threshold would become eligible for overtime pay at time-and-a-half when they work more than 40 hours a week. Under the 2016 rule the bill adopts, the Department of Labor estimated more than 13 million employees would be affected, including 4.2 million newly eligible for overtime and 8.9 million with stronger protections.

how_it_helps.text: Under the 2016 rule the bill adopts, more than 13 million employees would benefit — 4.2 million newly eligible for overtime and 8.9 million with strengthened protections.
The old $23,660 salary threshold was below the poverty line for a family of four, meaning many salaried managers and supervisors worked 50- or 60-hour weeks with no overtime pay at all.
The bill requires the threshold to be updated every three years automatically, without new rulemaking, so it keeps pace with wages instead of eroding for decades as it did after 1975.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of salaried workers who would newly owe overtime — chains and businesses in retail, restaurants, banking, insurance, and manufacturing that rely on salaried supervisors and managers. They would either pay time-and-a-half for long hours, cap those workers' hours, or raise their salaries above the threshold to keep them exempt.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face higher labor costs and would have to track hours for salaried staff, converting some salaried roles to hourly ones with less scheduling flexibility.

The threshold is pegged to the 40th percentile of the lowest-wage region of the country, which is a uniform national floor; some businesses argue a region-tied cutoff works poorly where local wages and living costs differ sharply from that region.
The increase would take effect quickly — the first month after the third month following enactment — giving employers little time to adjust payrolls or budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of salaried workers earning between $23,660 and roughly $47,476 who regularly work long unpaid hours, the gain is straightforward: legal overtime pay. The cost falls on their employers, and some of that cost could pass to workers through reduced hours, lower raises, or faster pressure to automate — a real risk, though the modest rate of increase compared to restoring the 1975 coverage level was a deliberate compromise. The main design weakness is that it fixes overtime through the salary cutoff alone, leaving the loophole that employers can retitle workers' duties rather than pay them more.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 11, 2019, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken: the bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

The bill was endorsed by the chamber's Democratic leadership — the Democratic whip (Durbin) and senators including Sanders, Warren, Klobuchar, and Harris were among its cosponsors — yet it never advanced in committee.

Its provisions mirror the 2016 overtime rule that a federal court invalidated, and the bill would restore that rule's $47,476 threshold rather than the lower $35,308 threshold the Labor Department proposed in 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of salaried workers — retail, restaurant, and other chains with salaried managers and supervisors — are better off because the bill died: they continue to pay the outdated $23,660 threshold and owe no overtime to workers above it, no matter how many hours they work.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case that the overtime salary threshold had eroded for decades and should be restored to the 2016 rule's level.

for.name: 20 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Democratic and independent senators backing the bill, including the Democratic whip and both Sanders and Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the caucus's support but no Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — in the 19 months it remained pending.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the 116th Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent, and there is no record of any Republican support; the bill was referred to a committee chaired by a Republican and died there without a vote.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, and other employers of salaried managers
industries.note: These businesses rely on salaried supervisors who work long hours without overtime; raising the threshold to about $47,476 would require paying those workers time-and-a-half, capping their hours, or raising their salaries. The workers' gain in pay is these employers' added cost.

industries.industry: Business lobbies (e.g., retail and restaurant trade associations)
industries.note: The bill would codify a court-invalidated 2016 rule that business groups had spent years opposing through comment and litigation, making the higher threshold statutory and harder to undo than a regulation.
Small employers with salaried staff just above the old threshold would face new overtime costs, while any of their employees under the threshold would gain overtime pay.
